idiom_name: for await over AsyncIterable with a MessageHandler<I, O> contract
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds nothing to the runtime mechanics but makes the contract explicit: declare a handler type (payload and reply types plus the context carrying correlation id and return address) and consume the transport's async iterable with for await, so the compiler checks that the service's reply type matches what the sender expects. The untyped payload must still be validated before it is cast to the domain type - the annotation is a claim about the wire format, not a verification of it. Prefer this form when the transport is iterator-based or in-process.
pitfalls: JSON.parse returns any: casting to the domain interface without runtime validation lets shape drift reach the service, so validate at the boundary.
A for await loop over a stream that never closes never returns; the worker must react to an AbortSignal or the process will not shut down.
Async iterables buffer while the consumer is slower than the producer: without transport backpressure the loop becomes an unbounded queue.

variants.name: NestJS @MessagePattern / @EventPattern handler method
variants.implementation_notes: Nest's microservice layer is the framework realization: a controller method decorated with @MessagePattern(pattern) is invoked with the decoded payload for request-response (the returned value, rejected promise or emitted Observable item becomes the reply) and @EventPattern(pattern) for one-way events, with the transporter (TCP, Redis, NATS, Kafka, MQTT) configurable underneath. The endpoint object is replaced by the decorated method; hand-written consumers remain the choice when the transport is not supported by Nest or when acknowledgement policy must be controlled per message.
pitfalls: A rejected promise in a @MessagePattern handler is surfaced to the caller as a transport error; if the application needs a dead-letter or error channel instead, the failure must be caught and published explicitly.

Handlers are instantiated through Nest's DI container, so connection side effects belong in lifecycle hooks, not in the constructor, and request-scoped providers cannot be injected into a default-scoped handler.
